African business leaders remain confident about growth, but converting that confidence into sustained performance will depend on how effectively organisations navigate economic uncertainty, geopolitical disruption, technological change and structural constraints, according to the 2026 KPMG Africa CEO Outlook.
The third edition of the KPMG Africa CEO Outlook examines the priorities shaping business leadership across the continent, from investment and growth expectations to emerging risks, artificial intelligence (AI), talent and sustainability.
The findings point to a business environment in which ambition remains strong, but execution is becoming increasingly important. While 66% of African CEOs are confident in the global economy, broadly in line with the global benchmark of 65%, confidence in their domestic economies stands at 72%. A further 79% are confident in the growth prospects of their own organisations.
This confidence is supported by recent performance, with 86% of African CEOs reporting revenue growth in their latest financial year. However, only 58% expect annual earnings growth of at least 2.5% over the next three years, compared with 68% globally, suggesting that translating revenue gains into sustained profitability remains a priority.
African businesses operate in an increasingly interconnected global environment, where geopolitical tensions, energy-market volatility, supply-chain disruptions, and shifting trade relationships can influence investment decisions and operating costs.
For African economies, these pressures coexist with significant opportunities. The continent’s energy resources, critical minerals, expanding consumer markets and potential to develop local manufacturing and value chains position it to benefit from changes in global investment and supply-chain strategies. Realising this potential, however, will depend on infrastructure, reliable energy, skills, connectivity and predictable regulatory environments.
Cybersecurity and data security, alongside supply-chain resilience, are the leading threats to growth among African CEOs, each cited by 31% of respondents. The integration of AI into operating models and workflows follows at 27%.
Investment priorities reflect the need to strengthen operational resilience. Some 45% of African CEOs are increasing investment in cybersecurity and digital-risk resilience, 36% in regulatory compliance and reporting, and 31% in AI integration.
The findings suggest that resilience is no longer simply about protecting organisations against disruption. It is increasingly a condition for growth, enabling businesses to adapt to changing market conditions, protect critical operations and make investment decisions with greater confidence.
For businesses operating across diverse African markets, this requires balancing immediate operational pressures with longer-term investment in infrastructure, technology, governance and capabilities.
Tola Adeyemi, Senior Partner & CEO - KPMG One Africa, said: “African businesses are demonstrating confidence in their ability to grow, but the next phase of growth will require more than ambition. Leaders must make deliberate choices about where to invest, how to strengthen resilience and how to build organisations that can adapt to disruption. The opportunity is to translate the continent’s resources, markets and entrepreneurial capacity into more productive, competitive and sustainable businesses.”
AI remains a strategic investment priority for African business leaders, with 72% of CEOs identifying it as a top investment priority, compared with 79% globally. Yet only 14% believe their organisations are moving at the right pace or ahead of AI developments, against 66% of global CEOs.
This 52-percentage-point gap highlights a central challenge: African businesses recognise AI’s potential, but many are still working to develop the capabilities required to deploy it effectively and at scale.
Expectations around returns also differ. While 48% of African CEOs expect AI investments to deliver returns within one to three years, compared with 71% globally, 42% expect returns after three years, against 12% globally.
The longer investment horizon may reflect the work required to strengthen underlying data capabilities, integrate AI into existing systems, establish appropriate governance and develop the skills needed to realise value. It also reinforces the importance of evaluating AI against tangible business outcomes rather than adoption alone.
The opportunity for African businesses is not simply to adopt new technology, but to use it to improve productivity, strengthen competitiveness and develop new products and services suited to local and regional markets.
Technology investment is also reshaping workforce strategies. Despite the growing role of AI in business operations, 84% of African CEOs expect headcount to increase over the next three years, compared with 89% globally.
At the same time, 86% intend to retain and retrain high-potential employees, 82% are redesigning roles, career paths and team structures for human-AI collaboration, and 74% are hiring AI and technology talent.
Skills remain a significant constraint, with 59% identifying workforce skills gaps, 58% citing AI upskilling and training, and 52% pointing to challenges in attracting and retaining talent.
These findings underline the relationship between technology adoption and workforce development. Businesses will need to invest in both if they are to translate digital ambition into productivity gains. For African economies, developing relevant skills and expanding access to technology capabilities will also be important to ensuring that digital transformation supports broader economic participation.
African CEOs are increasingly approaching sustainability through the lens of commercial performance, operational resilience and reporting readiness.
Almost half, or 48%, report embedding sustainability more deeply into core business strategy, compared with 63% globally. Meanwhile, 40% are narrowing their focus to sustainability issues most critical to business performance, against 21% globally.
Energy choices reflect the practical realities of operating across African markets. Some 41% of African CEOs prioritise energy demand optimisation, compared with 37% globally; 40% plan to diversify towards renewable or lower-carbon external energy supply, compared with 49% globally; and 15% plan to add dedicated generation or storage capacity, against 13% globally.
Reporting readiness provides one of the clearest year-on-year indicators in the findings. The proportion of African CEOs who say their organisations have the capability to meet new sustainability reporting requirements has risen from 55% in the previous year to 65% in 2026.
The improvement points to progress in organisational preparedness, although the broader challenge remains embedding sustainability into business decisions in ways that support resilience, efficiency and long-term value creation.
